title: A Right With No Way to Sue Is Half a Right
hook: A prisoner's religious rights were violated and the harm was already done. The hard legal question was not whether it was wrong — it was whether he could recover anything at all.
key_points: A legal right needs a remedy: some relief a court can actually order once the violation has happened.
Injunctions stop ongoing conduct, but they do nothing for a harm that is finished — only damages reach backwards.
Damon Landor, a Rastafarian, had his dreadlocks shaved by Louisiana prison staff despite a religious-liberty claim; by the time he sued, no order could undo it.
The dispute reached the Supreme Court as a question about whether a religious-liberty statute allows suits for money against officials personally.
Writing at SCOTUSblog, Richard Garnett unpacks how remedies, statutory text and government immunity stack up in the case.
The general point: whether you can sue, and whom, often decides more than whether the right exists.
content_html: Lawyers have a saying: a right without a remedy is not much of a right. Courts can order someone to stop doing something, but an injunction only reaches conduct that is ongoing. When the harm is already complete, the only relief left is money — and whether money is available depends on the precise statute and on the immunities that shield governments and their employees.
extra_html:
Damon Landor's case put that abstraction in concrete form. Landor, a Rastafarian who had not cut his hair for years as a religious observance, had his dreadlocks shaved by Louisiana prison staff. Nothing a court could order afterward would restore them, so his suit turned on whether the federal statute protecting prisoners' religious exercise permits a damages claim against officials in their individual capacity.

Writing at SCOTUSblog, Notre Dame law professor Richard Garnett walks through the layers this stacks up: what the statute's text authorizes, how Congress's spending power shapes the remedies that come with it, and where sovereign immunity cuts off suits against a state itself. The takeaway generalizes well beyond prisons — in American public law, the fight over whom you may sue is often the whole fight.

related.title: "Clearly Established" Law and Qualified Immunity
related.hook: A right you hold on paper can be unenforceable in court: officials escape damages unless a prior ruling already said, in nearly identical facts, that what they did was illegal.

related.title: Civil Liberties Basics
related.hook: The freedoms that protect individuals from overreach by the state — like speech, belief, and a fair trial.

related.title: Due Process
related.hook: Due process is the promise that the state can't take your liberty or property on a whim — it must follow fair, known rules before it acts against you.

related.title: Exonerated Isn't the Same as Compensated
related.hook: Getting a conviction thrown out does not get you paid. In most states you must then prove your innocence all over again — to a higher standard, against a state that may still call you guilty.

flashcards.prompt: Why can an injunction be useless to someone whose rights were already violated?
flashcards.back_html: An injunction stops ongoing or future conduct. For a harm that is finished, only damages offer any relief at all.

flashcards.prompt: What made Landor's case turn on remedies rather than on whether a right was violated?

choices.text: The harm was complete, so the question became whether he could sue officials for money
The prison denied that any religious practice was involved
He had not yet been released, so no court could hear him

flashcards.explanation_html: His dreadlocks had already been cut. No order could restore them, which pushed the case onto whether damages were available.

flashcards.prompt: What does 'a right without a remedy' mean in practice?
flashcards.back_html: A right courts recognize but cannot enforce with any relief you can actually obtain — so violating it carries no consequence.
